cues.text: Let's finish this session with some additional independent Agile practice, and we'll work through three short scenarios that test how well you can apply what you've learned.
First, consider a maintenance team.
This team receives unpredictable incidents alongside its regular feature work.
Think about what that means: work does not arrive in a neat, planned batch.
Incidents turn up at random times, and they compete for attention with the features the team is also building.
In a situation like this, Kanban with WIP limits and an explicit expedited-work policy can accommodate variable arrivals.
Let's unpack that.
Kanban is a flow-based approach, and WIP stands for work in progress.
A WIP limit caps how many items can be in a stage at once, so the team does not start more than it can finish.
An explicit expedited-work policy states clearly, in advance, how urgent items such as serious incidents are handled when they arrive.
Together, these let the team absorb work that comes in at an unpredictable rate.
Now compare that with a different kind of team.
A product team pursuing a cohesive two-week outcome may choose Scrum.
Here the work is organised around a single, coherent goal for a fixed two-week period, and that fits the Scrum approach.
Notice the wording: the team "may choose" Scrum.
The source presents this as a reasonable choice, not an absolute rule.
Whichever you pick, there is an important caution.
Neither choice removes the need for quality gates, customer feedback or planning.
Choosing Kanban does not mean you can skip planning, and choosing Scrum does not guarantee quality.
Both still need checkpoints that work must pass, both still need feedback from customers, and both still need planning.
One more practical point.
Imagine a blocked review column on the board.
That suggests the team should resolve review capacity before pulling more work.
In other words, if finished work is piling up waiting for review, starting new items only makes the pile bigger.
The sensible response is to fix the review bottleneck first, and only then pull new work.
Now the second scenario, a product that is evolving.
Picture a product that begins as basic parcel tracking and grows to include alerts and exception management.
Each newly delivered usable capability is an increment.
So the step from tracking to alerts is an increment, and the later addition of exception management is another increment.
Each one adds something the user can actually use.
Contrast that with what happens when the team changes something that already exists.
Revising the tracking interface after feedback is iterative refinement.
The capability is already there, and the team improves it in response to what users said.
This is a useful way to keep the two ideas apart: an increment adds a new usable capability, while iterative refinement revises something already delivered, guided by feedback.
As the product grows, the parts must keep working together.
Protect integration with automated regression and shared contracts.
Automated regression checks confirm that earlier behaviour still works after new changes, and shared contracts give the different parts of the product an agreed definition of how they interact.
Next, a point about reporting progress.
Use burnup to expose scope increases rather than hide them in a burndown graph.
A burnup chart shows the work completed and the total scope as separate lines, so when scope grows, you can see it.
A burndown graph can hide that growth, because added scope may simply look like slower progress.
Finally, the retrospective.
A retrospective experiment should identify one actionable improvement, an owner and an observation period.
That means exactly one improvement the team can act on, a named person responsible for it, and a defined period during which the team watches whether it works.
To recap this practice set: Kanban with WIP limits suits variable arrivals, Scrum suits a cohesive two-week outcome, and neither removes quality gates, customer feedback or planning.
Increments add usable capability, iterative refinement improves what exists, burnup reveals scope growth, and every retrospective experiment needs one improvement, an owner and an observation period.
